extracted.intended_audience: readers and practitioners of literary criticism; poets and educated general readers interested in epic poetry and genteel conduct in writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging and composing the 'sentiments' (thoughts, speeches, and behaviour) in epic poems and for adapting critical tone to different audiences; focuses on what thoughts are proper, sublime, natural, or to be avoided. Also includes advice on polite raillery and treating faults in writing for particular readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments must conform to characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sentiments in an Epic Poem are the Thoughts and Behaviour which the Author ascribes to the Persons whom he introduces, and are just when they are conformable to the characters of the several Persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether what a character says or does fits that character's established nature; special praise when a poet invents characters (e.g., Milton) and still gives them apt sentiments. Example contrast: easier for Homer to find proper sentiments for known Grecian generals than for Milton to invent Adam and Eve's conversational sentiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments must suit the subject (relation to things)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Sentiments have likewise a relation to Things as well as Persons, and are then perfect when they are such as are adapted to the Subject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the thoughts and speech are appropriate not only to the speaker but to the overall theme and scope of the epic; misfitting sentiments reduce the poem's propriety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentiments should be proper for the intended emotional ends
rubrics_metrics.description: If the poet endeavours to argue or explain, to magnify or diminish, to raise Love or Hatred, Pity or Terror, or any other Passion, we ought to consider whether the Sentiments he makes use of are proper for those Ends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether particular lines and speeches effectively produce the intended emotional effect (pity, terror, admiration, etc.); a thought may be suitable in one aim but inappropriate in another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pursue both natural and sublime sentiments
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of Sentiments, the Natural and the Sublime, which are always to be pursued in an Heroic Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An epic should include thoughts that feel natural (fit human nature and conversation) and also lift the reader by sublimity — greatness of ideas. Milton is praised for sublimity; Virgil for propriety and naturalness. Strive for both where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer sublimity and greatness of thought in epic
rubrics_metrics.description: Milton's chief Talent, and indeed his distinguishing Excellence, lies in the Sublimity of his Thoughts... It is impossible for the Imagination of Man to distend itself with greater Ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sublimity (grand, transporting ideas) is a central aim of epic poetry; poets should attempt extraordinary, elevating conceptions especially in key books/passages (e.g., creation, councils, great speeches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid affected and unnatural thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of Thoughts which are carefully to be avoided. The first are such as are affected and unnatural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of artificial, overly refined conceits and 'swelling' or vain embellishments that do not arise naturally from character or subject. The modern false refinements (as in some later poets) are cited as vices to avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mean and vulgar thoughts
rubrics_metrics.description: The second [kind of Thoughts to be avoided are] such as are mean and vulgar. An Epic Poet should not only avoid such Sentiments as are unnatural or affected, but also such as are mean and vulgar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low, groveling, or homely sentiments that provoke laughter are generally inappropriate in the heroic/epic strain; such material undermines the poem's dignity. Homer’s occasional homeliness is explained by his era, but in general these are faults in epic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit burlesque or mirth in epic to appropriately timed moments
rubrics_metrics.description: Sentiments which raise Laughter can very seldom be admitted with any Decency into an Heroic Poem... The only Piece of Pleasantry in Paradise Lost is...a String of Punns, which I look upon to be the most exceptionable in the whole Poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If comic or burlesque passages are used, they must be sparing and well-timed (e.g., Virgil's single laugh in the fifth book is excused because it occurs among games and diversions). Otherwise, humour or puns risk damaging epic majesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate sentiments in light of historical vs invented characters' difficulty
rubrics_metrics.description: Homer and Virgil introduced persons whose characters are commonly known... Milton's characters, most of them, lie out of Nature, and were to be formed purely by his own Invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be conscious that inventing entirely new, non-historical characters (as Milton did) raises the difficulty of supplying apt sentiments — this is a factor when assessing a poet's success or failure in character-speech congruity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt critical tone to the quality and way of life of subjects (polite raillery)
rubrics_metrics.description: You should take along with you the Distinction of Manners of the World, according to the Quality and Way of Life of the Persons concerned... A Man of Breeding speaks of even Misfortune among Ladies without giving it the most terrible Aspect it can bear: And this Tenderness towards them is much more to be preserved when you speak of Vices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticizing or satirizing persons (especially women in the essay's context), tailor severity to the audience and the subject's social standing; avoid shocking or needlessly harsh descriptions that will disgust readers of the intended circle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit depiction of vices for a genteel (tea-table) audience
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not necessary when you write to the Tea-table, that you should draw Vices which carry all the Horror of Shame and Contempt: If you paint an impertinent Self-love, an artful Glance, an assumed Complexion, you say all which you ought to suppose they can possibly be guilty of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For lighter, sociable readerships, prefer mild, recognizable faults over scandalous, shocking depictions. The aim is to provoke assent and shared raillery rather than disgust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of polite raillery: speak of faults as if you loved the person
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule of polite Raillery, is to speak of a Man's Faults as if you loved him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gentle, affectionate phrasing in satire — this keeps rebuke social and effective. Example: do not term a man guilty of occasional intemperance a 'drunkard'; employ milder, reparative labels (anecdote of Caesar calling someone 'a careless fellow').

rubrics_metrics.name: Writers should tailor discourse to entertain their target readers
rubrics_metrics.description: It is therefore expected from every Writer, to treat his Argument in such a Manner, as is most proper to entertain the sort of Readers to whom his Discourse is directed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always consider your intended readership's sensibilities and expectations when choosing what to include and how to phrase it; inappropriate tone risks alienating the audience who could otherwise support or echo your raillery.
